body: Taiwan uses Traditional Chinese, a complex script with intricate characters. This script is also used in Hong Kong and shares some characters with Japanese.

Poles in Taiwan almost always feature black and yellow diagonal-striped markings that run all the way to the bottom. While South Korea has similar markings, they are much shorter and do not reach the ground.
Taiwan drives on the right side of the road, which distinguishes it from Japan and Hong Kong, where they drive on the left.
Roads in Taiwan generally feature double yellow middle lines with single white outer lines. Thinner roads sometimes use a single dashed yellow line instead.
Roads with only white outer lines and no middle lines are common in Taiwan and can be a very good clue for identification.
Red outer lines that indicate no parking are a common and essentially unique feature of Taiwan, especially in cities.
Taiwan uses black on yellow chevrons.
Mirrors with orange hoods are frequently featured at intersections and on bends in Taiwan.
Taiwan uses bollards with two or three circular reflectors on a black rectangle, and 'lollipop' reflectors on guardrails, similar to Japan.
Concrete drainage ditches are commonly found on the side of roads in Taiwan.
Box-like distribution transformers, mostly painted dark green or grey, are frequently found in Taiwan, especially in urban areas.
Taiwanese architecture often features boxy residential buildings, walls covered in white tiles, and light green tin sheds.
In Generation 3 coverage, you can find a black car with a long antenna and a central red brake light, similar to a car seen in Russia.
Some Generation 3 coverage in Taiwan features a car with a very large blur that can resemble low-cam, although the camera height is normal.
Be aware of Taiwan's several outlying islands with Street View coverage, including Kinmen, Matsu, Penghu, Green Island, and Orchid Island.
Taiwan telephone numbers have a 2-digit area code from 02 to 08 that generally increases as you go south. Mobile numbers start with 09.
Taiwan's National Freeway system uses odd numbers for north-south routes and even numbers for east-west routes, with numbers generally increasing from west to east and north to south.
On township road signs, the Chinese character written before or above the road number indicates the county.
Many utility poles in Taiwan have blue plaques with alphanumeric codes that act as a precise coordinate system, which can be used to pinpoint a location.
The central-western part of Taiwan consists of a plain with flat to low rolling terrain, where crops and farmland are common.
The central-eastern two-thirds of Taiwan is dominated by forested mountains, where higher elevations can feature less tropical, temperate, or even coniferous trees.
The Hualien-Taitung Valley on the east coast is a long, flat plain recognizable by the densely forested mountains that surround it to the east and west.
The Yilan Plain is a flat, open area identifiable by mountain ranges to the north, west, and south, but with no mountains to the east.
The island of Kinmen is recognizable by trees with fuzzy leaves lining the roads and red-tinged soil, with only Generation 3 coverage available.
The Miaoli and Hsinchu regions share a landscape of low rolling hills, winding roads, and sparse, sometimes unkempt-looking farmland.
Taichung is characterized by open plains surrounded by low mountains, which are often visible in the distance.
Areca palms (or betel nut palms) are extensively found in the mountainous regions of central and southern Taiwan.
Coconut palms are primarily found along the coast in the southern half of Taiwan.
Norfolk Island pines are extremely common in Penghu county, often planted in tightly packed rows alongside roads.
Distinctive leafless trees are most frequently seen in Penghu.
Cultivated fish farms are mostly found along the western coast in the southern half of Taiwan, predominantly in Yunlin, Chiayi, Tainan, and Kaohsiung counties.
Tea plantations are a common sight in the mountainous areas of Taiwan, especially in Chiayi, Nantou, Hsinchu, and Miaoli.
Stands selling betel nuts are a common sight along roads in Taiwan, often featuring colorful, bright lights to attract customers.
